narrative:
The model estimated a 95% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. For your application, that estimate was treated as a strong sign of academic risk, so your admission was denied. The assessment did not use your gender or race.

The decision was driven most strongly by your third-year class standing. You were in the first decile in Year 3, compared with an accepted-student average around the sixth decile. That very low third-year rank was the largest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. The next most influential factor was your family income bracket: coming from a middle-income family added to the risk signal, although its influence was smaller. Third was your first-year class standing. You were in the second decile in Year 1, compared with an accepted-student average around the sixth decile, and this also pushed the estimate toward failure. Together, these factors outweighed any positive signals in your profile.

To move forward, request admissions feedback and ask whether any contextual explanation of your academic record could be reconsidered. Focus on strengthening the areas the review found concerning, especially upper-year academic performance, and consider retaking the LSAT if you can improve it. You may also apply to programs that review applicants more holistically and allow you to explain your academic trajectory.
